audio_caption: Two males introduce themselves. The first man speaks about coordinating search and rescue teams. He refers to himself as head of mission. The second man states that he was always a part of the winch team, sometimes as a captain. A female asks about the history of Yuventa, asking when it was born and why.

The clip opens with a male speaker discussing how it began as "more a campaign than a proper search and rescue effort," mentioning young people from Berlin being involved in welcoming moments in Germany in 2015 and the goal of being recognized. The speaker sounds informative and slightly reflective. He mentions they had a ship and asked people to join the crew. He transitions to mentioning that they managed to rescue more than 1,000 people.  Another male speaker continues, saying that 15 other missions followed, totaling 16 missions in one year, until the ship was seized in August 2017. He adds that they saved over 14,000 lives, and that "every person who doesn't die" is a reason to go out and do this work. The final speaker is female, and only utters a brief sound.

The audio clip begins with a discussion of rescue operations at sea, where the speaker notes, "rescue missions didn't change," emphasizing the unchanging technical aspects, but highlighting a shift in behavior from European, particularly Italian, authorities that "repress" and hinder the ships with new strategies to stop the sea rescue. The atmosphere shifts as the speaker finds it "horrible when people die out there" but even more so when facing "stupid trial." Another speaker concurs, noting "two major changes." The audio then closes out with speech and some subtle background activity.

The audio clip begins with one male speaker discussing "the Libyan coast guard" and their presence, describing their involvement in rescues. He says they not only intervene in rescues but also "managed to kidnap" people from boats, forcing them back to Libya in high numbers. He characterizes this as "quite a major change." Another male speaker responds with, "the."

The clip starts with a male speaker talking about administrative and legal aspects that prevented chips from going out. He mentions Savini's role in not allowing ships to enter the port, and subsequent phases where ships could enter but not leave, leading to them being stuck for months, mainly due to technical administrative reasons. He then speaks about the after the Curo disaster and mentions the Piantedosi decree, making it even harder to operate, particularly the policy of assigning rescue ships to ports of safety further north after rescues, causing delays in transferring people. He also mentions detentions and rules in the decree leading to detentions of at least 20 days.

The clip starts with a conversational exchange, featuring a question about a rescue mission abortion and authorities placing hidden microphones on a ship, posed in an inquisitive tone. A male voice confirms these claims, recounting the events of May 2017 during a rescue operation with multiple NGO ships. He speaks of being instructed to transfer people to a safe port, which was initially denied. Following negotiations and pressure, they were allowed to transfer only a portion of the people, later instructed by the MCC Rome to take the remainder to Lampedusa. He adds that NGOs present at the scene called for help, stating they were overwhelmed. Ultimately, the response was that help would be sent.

The audio clip features two distinct male speakers. The first one speaks about their arrival at Lampedusa, describing the events as initially fast-paced. The second speaker elaborates on a situation involving distress calls from numerous boats over a three-day period and says that some of the boats disappeared, possibly with up to 1000 people, and then poses questions regarding rescue operations and restrictions. The tone is urgent and concerned as they convey the gravity of the situation at sea.

The clip starts with a female speaker inquiring about the role of the National Antimafia Directorate in the management of Europe's southern maritime border, speaking in a neutral and informative tone. She's followed by a male speaker, who recommends that everyone read an article from Lorenzo D'Agostino in the Intercept.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing anti-mafia prosecution in Italy, particularly its role in cracking down on smuggling networks. He mentions identifying Libyan smuggling networks as a new target and a new kind of mafia, and how they use techniques from their fight against the mafia such as going for "the small fishes and then going up the ladder and finding the the bigger fishes".

The audio features a male speaker discussing the use of "Magenostrum ships" and "Magenostrum operation" in placing "police officers" on rescue ships to conduct interviews immediately after rescues. He mentions the plan was "to use the most vulnerable moment" to ask questions about who was driving the boat, leading to numerous arrests. He says they identified people steering boats or holding the compass as part of a smuggling network, although they were aware they were people on the move themselves and not part of the network. His tone is informative and somewhat critical.

The audio clip features one male speaker, discussing how civil fleets, by laying out their own rescue missions, disrupted certain "police actions." He mentions that this is one reason why they were targeted as an "enemy" and explains that there were two ideas: placing police officers on ships, which was part of a code of conduct, and blaming them for colluding with smugglers. He says that they would then use legal means to stop their missions, leaving them with a clear field of operations.

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing his case, stating that it's "good for the statistics against smugglers" but asserting that those he helped are not smugglers themselves, but people seeking "freedom," "life" and that "they have the right to come to Europe." He explains that he and others are being charged with aiding illegal immigration, noting that there are "21 persons charged". He points out the irony, stating that they are charged for "helping people to immigrate illegal to Italy and it is not illegal to come to Europe and ask for Asylum". The speaker speaks clearly, but is obviously frustrated with the charges.
